#1768. Arsenal lose second successive pre-season friendly after parading Guimaraes

Arsenal suffered back-to-back pre-season defeats as they lost 3-2 to Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup on Sunday.

The loss to the German side followed a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis on Wednesday night in Dublin.

Before kick-off, Bruno Guimarães was paraded to the Arsenal faithful after completing his £75m move from Newcastle on Saturday.

But enthusiasm about the Brazilian’s arrival was dampened when Dortmund took the lead at the Emirates inside the opening 10 minutes. Felix Nmecha’s incisive pass into the penalty area was met by the run of Samuele Inácio, who made no mistake with a clinical finish into the far corner.

The Bundesliga side doubled their lead just before the half-hour mark as 18-year-old Greek international Konstantinos Karetsas curled one in from the edge of the box.

Ten minutes after half-time, Arsenal pulled a goal back through Ethan Nwaneri, who scored from Christos Tzolis’s cross. However, moments later Dortmund restored their two-goal advantage as Joane Gadou smashed home from a corner.

Arsenal kept their hopes alive through a Viktor Gyokeres penalty after Tzolis was brought down, but Dortmund were able to hold on to claim victory. After the full-time whistle, there was a penalty shoot-out, which Arsenal won 5-4.

Arsenal still have a number of players to return to action following their World Cup exploits, including Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke. England and Real Madrid midfielder Jude Bellingham was in attendance at the Emirates to watch his younger brother Jobe in action for Dortmund.

As well as Guimarães, there was another addition on display at the Emirates: Arsenal have added last year’s title win to the list of honours displayed inside the stadium.

Arsenal play Cesc Fàbregas’s Como on Wednesday, before taking on Manchester City in the Community Shield next weekend. Mikel Arteta’s side then start the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly promoted Coventry City.

Nwaneri steps up with the chance to win the shootout and does so with aplomb, sending Meyer the wrong way, and Arsenal win the shootout 5-4.

The former Chelsea man receives some boos as he steps up but calmly slots home to keep Dortmund’s hopes alive.

Meyer goes the right way but there is far too much power on this penalty from Martinelli. Meyer had no chance of saving that one.

We have the first penalty miss of this shootout as Meslier guesses the right way and saves what was a pretty poor penalty from Albert. Advantage Arsenal.

A few stutters in the run-up but Hincapie slots home into the bottom left corner, with Meyer going the wrong way.

He came on right at the end of the game to take a penalty and rewards the decision from his manager to do so as he lifts it over Meslier diving to his left.

Another penalty scored in the left corner. Meyer again guesses the right way but cannot prevent Vieira.

There is a bit of a stutter in the run-up as Reggiani stares down Meslier and sends the Arsenal keeper the wrong way, finding the same corner as Sabitzer and Jesus.

Meyer in the Dortmund goal guesses the right way but Jesus lifts it over him with a quality penalty.

Meslier takes an age to get ready but Sabitzer does not care, sending the Arsenal keeper the wrong way and emphatically finding the left corner.

Right, we are ready for penalties. Dortmund will take first, with Sabitzer to take their opening penalty up against Meslier.

Arsenal have the ball in the net in the final few seconds and think they have a very late equaliser but Martinelli’s effort is ruled out for an offside. Meyer will be a relieved man in the Dortmund goal as he allowed Martinelli’s shot to go through him.

The final whistle is then blown and Dortmund have beaten Arsenal 3-2 to take the Emirates Cup.

It is perhaps not a massive surprise but the game has lost some flow with all the changes both sides have made during this second half.

There is set to be a penalty shootout at the end of this one, no matter what the final result is.

With just under 15 minutes to go at the Emirates, Arsenal are going to make a number of changes. Plenty of youngsters are entering the fray as are a few experienced players like Jesus and Martinelli.

The Swede sends Meyer the wrong way and slots into the bottom right corner. It is now 3-2 and this game is not over with 20 minutes to go.

Tzolis goes down inside the Dortmund penalty area and referee Chris Kavanagh points to the spot. He was caught inside the box and there did not appear to be too many complaints from the visitors.

Nwaneri comes close to getting his second goal of the half. Tzolis rolls it across the face of the penalty area to Nwaneri, who hits it first time and forces Meyer into a good save to his right, pushing it onto the post.

In the aftermath of that Dortmund goal, there are a raft of changes for both sides. Arsenal have brought on Salmon and Hincapie for Calafiori and Gabriel.

Dortmund have brought on the experience of the likes of Sabitzer and Guirassy.

Arsenal had some problems from corners the other day against Betis and they concede minutes after getting a goal back. Arsenal fail to deal with a corner from the right and the ball ends up with Gadou at the back post. Gadou takes one touch before finding the net, despite the best efforts of numerous Arsenal defenders on the line.

Should Inacio have gone down? The young Italian is played in behind the Arsenal defence and has Calafiori all over his back. Inacio ends up losing possession on the edge of the Arsenal penalty area but had he gone down Calafiori could have been in trouble.

Mikel Arteta’s side reduce Dortmund’s lead to just the one goal. Tzolis cuts it back from the left side of the box and picks out Nwaneri eight yards out from goal in the centre of the box. Nwaneri makes no mistake, smashing home and Arsenal are back in this game.

White is found on the right side of the box but is denied by Meyer in the Dortmund goal. The subsequent corner comes to nothing.

Dortmund have brought on former Chelsea and Aston Villa man Chukwuemeka on at the break. Arsenal have made an alteration at the break with Meslier replacing Kepa in goal.

During half-time at the Emirates, the official song of the 2026 Fifa World Cup Dai Dai by Shakira and Burna Boy is being belted out over the tannoy. Two added minutes at the end of this first half.

What a finish that is to put the German side 2-0 up! 18-year-old Karetsas, who has joined Dortmund from Genk this summer, is afforded too much space outside the Arsenal penalty area as he drives towards the box and punishes the hosts for that, curling a sublime shot into the far corner.

Odegaard slides a clever pass into the right channel to pick out the run of Gyokeres towards the Dortmund box. Mane though slides in with a perfectly-timed challenge to take it off Gyokeres. Mane had to time that right with the challenge being right on the edge of his own box.

Arsenal hit the bar. Dowman does well down Arsenal’s right to drive into the Dortmund box and cuts it back to Gyokeres. The Swedish striker takes a few touches before getting his shot away, which clips the top of the bar.

A dangerous cross from the left comes all the way to Svensson at the back post but he lacked conviction with his header and it goes wide. Perhaps he should be hitting the target.

Down at the other end Arsenal have a headed chance of their own. Havertz clips in a cross from the left and picks out Gyokeres. The Swede is a fair way out from goal and his header goes wide.

Should Havertz have done better with this opportunity? The German is played in down the right channel and has Gyokeres calling for the cross in space in the centre of the box. Havertz tries to find him but Meyer is out to smother it. Had Havertz found Gyokeres, it would likely have been a simple tap-in for the Swede.

Odegaard appears to be through one-on-one but then goes down just outside the Dortmund box. Mane pleads his innocence but referee Chris Kavanagh does not agree, giving a free-kick. If this was a competitive game, Mane would potentially have been sent off.

Gyokeres will take and opts for power over accuracy. It is safe to say his effort is terrible, blazing over the bar and missing the target by some margin.

Calafiori trips Bellingham as Dortmund attempted to counter. If this was a competitive fixture, Calafiori likely would have been booked for that foul.

Bellingham and Havertz are involved in quite the collision. Both players go for the header and Havertz just gets to it first. Havertz is awarded the foul and is ok.

The German side take the lead inside the opening seven minutes. Nmecha slides a lovely pass through the Arsenal defensive line to pick out the run of Inacio into the Arsenal penalty area. It is a clinical finish from Inacio, who slides his effort into the far corner,

Dortmund’s first proper foray forward causes Arsenal issues and Tzolis is forced to put it behind for Dortmund’s first corner of the game. The inswinger though to the front post is poor and Gyokeres easily heads away from danger.

Counting down until kick-off ⏰ Make sure you're in your seats by 1.45pm (UK), Gooners - we have a very special guest in store 👀

When Bruno Guimarães signed for Newcastle United from Lyon in January 2022, much was made of the idea that he had rejected Arsenal in favour of a move to St James’ Park. The Brazilian played along with it, posting a video on his social media pages which featured multiple newspaper headlines about Arsenal wanting to buy him.

The Newcastle fans, still delirious about the recent takeover by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, understandably lapped it up. Their dream was to overthrow the established powers in English football, and the capture of Guimarães was regarded as a sign that they were truly ready to challenge teams of Arsenal’s stature and wealth.

Even the lyrics to the midfielder’s chant referred to the north Londoners, as Newcastle fans sang that Guimarães “could have signed for Arsenal” but chose instead to play “in the famous black and white”.

Yesterday Arsenal announced the signing of Brazilian midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle for £75m on a four-year deal, with the option of a further year. Here is what the Brazilian had to say:

“I feel good, I feel amazing. I am glad for the opportunity. Since the first time I spoke to (Andrea) Berta and Mikel (Arteta) I was excited. I just felt inside of me that I need a new challenge in my life and I think to be an Arsenal player is going to be an exciting challenge in my life.

“I think after playing two World Cups, I am at the point of my life, I think I need a challenge like this. I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I am in the right place to do it. I am so excited to start. We have tough games to play this season so the squad is going to be very, very important and I am hopeful we can achieve our dreams.”

Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

“I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

“I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”

This is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

#1767. AC Milan devise £53m Endrick transfer plan with Real Madrid buy-back clause

By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 14:51

AC Milan are reportedly preparing a new approach to sign Real Madrid forward Endrick in January, with a proposed buy-back arrangement designed to convince the Spanish giants to sanction his departure.

The Italian club have previously explored a loan move for the 20-year-old Brazilian, who has struggled for regular playing time under Jose Mourinho despite showing considerable promise during his spell at Lyon last season.

However, Milan are now considering a more ambitious proposal that could see Endrick eventually join them on a permanent basis while allowing Madrid to retain control over his long-term future.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the Rossoneri are weighing up an initial loan with an option or obligation to buy for approximately €60m (£53m), plus bonuses.

Crucially, the agreement would also include a buy-back clause worth around €80m (£70m), giving Real Madrid the opportunity to bring Endrick back to the Santiago Bernabeu if he develops into the player they believe he can become.

The proposed structure resembles Madrid's arrangement with Como for Nico Paz and could provide a potential solution to the disagreements that have previously prevented Endrick from leaving.

Milan's interest in Endrick is not new, but their latest reported strategy represents a change from the short-term loan previously considered.

Rather than simply borrowing the striker for six months, the Serie A club would be prepared to make a substantial financial commitment while offering Madrid assurances over the player's future.

An eventual €60m purchase would represent a major investment for Milan, who are expected to have around €70m available for the January transfer window.

The proposed €80m buy-back clause would give Madrid the possibility of reversing a permanent departure, although there is currently no indication that the Spanish club have accepted the arrangement.

There is also uncertainty over whether Milan would seek an obligation to buy or merely an option, with Italian reports discussing both possibilities.

Either structure would require an agreement over the conditions attached to the purchase and Madrid's subsequent right to re-sign the player.

Real have so far been reluctant to sanction Endrick's exit despite his limited opportunities.

Mourinho has publicly expressed his desire to retain the Brazilian, acknowledging that he has found it difficult to provide him with the playing time his development requires.

Endrick has made only limited appearances this season, contributing one goal and one assist in 141 minutes of football.

His situation follows a productive loan spell at Lyon during the 2025-26 campaign, when he registered eight goals and seven assists in 21 appearances.

Those performances demonstrated his ability to make an impact with regular minutes, strengthening interest from clubs seeking attacking reinforcements.

Real Madrid's previous reluctance to approve a permanent move for Endrick has complicated Milan's efforts, but the inclusion of a buy-back clause could offer a different basis for negotiations.

Milan may also have an advantage through their connections with Endrick's representatives.

Club owner Gerry Cardinale reportedly maintains a positive relationship with Roc Nation, the agency responsible for the Brazilian's career.

Cardinale had already expressed an interest in bringing Endrick to San Siro during the summer and is said to have requested updates whenever Madrid make a definitive decision about the youngster's future.

Former Milan and Real Madrid midfielder Kaka could also become involved in attempts to persuade Endrick to consider the move.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the Brazilian legend is viewed as a potentially influential figure because of his connections with both clubs and his standing in Brazilian football.

There is no confirmation that Kaka has formally entered negotiations or spoken directly to Endrick about joining Milan.

Nevertheless, his possible involvement adds another dimension to the club's pursuit.

Another former Milan favourite, Ronaldinho, has also offered an encouraging assessment of Endrick's ability to succeed in Italian football.

Speaking in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport, the 2005 Ballon d'Or winner insisted that his compatriot possesses the qualities required to adapt to Serie A.

"He is a player who can play anywhere in the world," Ronaldinho said.

"He has played in different leagues and done well, in France, Brazil and Spain. He is very young and can play well, yes."

Ronaldinho's comments were an assessment of Endrick's qualities rather than an indication that he is involved in Milan's transfer plans.

The Rossoneri face competition from Roma, where Gian Piero Gasperini is also interested in strengthening his attacking options.

The capital club have been linked with a January loan, while interest from England and France has also been reported.

However, a recent report from Corriere dello Sport suggested that Endrick was not particularly enthusiastic about moving to Milan, potentially presenting another obstacle even if the clubs can agree financial terms.

Milan are therefore maintaining alternative options, with Club Brugge striker Nicolo Tresoldi also under consideration.

The 22-year-old has scored 14 goals in 17 appearances this season and is reportedly valued at approximately €60m (£53m).

Brugge would prefer to retain Tresoldi until the summer, meaning Milan could explore signing one of their attacking targets in January before returning for the other at the end of the campaign.

For Endrick, the decisive factor remains Real Madrid's willingness to reconsider their position. Milan's proposed buy-back arrangement may offer a compromise, but no formal agreement has been reached and Mourinho has not changed his publicly stated desire to keep the striker.

#1766. Is the Gyokeres iron hot enough for Hull?

I’m here for our book launch which takes place tonight, but also for our game against Hull tomorrow. Mikel Arteta will meet the press this afternoon ahead of that one, and we’ll bring you all the stories on Arseblog News. I don’t think there’s gonna be anything mind-blowing, it looked like we came through the Slavia Prague game without any issues, so fingers crossed that’s the case.

I suppose I’m mildly curious as to whether Viktor Gyokeres’ performance on Wednesday will see him keep his place up front. He got a great goal, provided an assist for Noni Madueke, and probably should have had another assist when he headed back across goal for Mikel Merino, only for the Spaniard to head over the bar when we know he can do better from those situations.

He’s a player who seems to need confidence and rhythm, and on that basis it would make some sense to keep him in the starting line-up. After the last Interlull, when he scored in four successive games for Sweden, I made the case that giving him a start in our first game back would make some sense to try and harness some of what was a good goal scoring run. Strike while the iron is hot and all that.

I looked at a home game against Leeds as the kind of fixture that would suit him. He scored two against them at home last season, and one at Elland Road, but when the time came Mikel Arteta picked Kai Havertz up front. Speaking about the decision to start Gyokeres on Wednesday in Prague, the manager said:

It was a game we believed would be really good for him, for the demands the opponent puts in and the spaces he could use. He’s done it really well, not just for the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s really great news for him, because he really needed that performance.

The question will be does Arteta think Hull at home will be as good for him as Slavia Prague away? After a bright start to the season they haven’t won any of their last seven but they have drawn five of those. Chances are they’re going to come and sit deep, using the blueprint we’ve seen many teams deploy against Arsenal in the past. If a Gyokeres game, if we can call it that, requires the opposition to leave spaces he can use (as per Arteta’s quote above), then maybe this isn’t one of those.

However, on paper, and with all due respect to tomorrow’s opposition, if Hull at home isn’t a Gyokeres game, then it’s hard not to be a bit worried. Personally, I’d be all right to see him start this one, and if it doesn’t work then you have other options. Havertz is the obvious one, but Mikel Merino is an alternative as well with his ability to find spaces inside the opponent’s penalty area. Ideally though, it’s a bit of a building block of a game for the Swedish international. We need him to deliver goals and assists, the last few weeks have been a bit more positive in that regard, and ultimately it’s important that the manager recognises the moments in a season when he might have to choose one player over another for the overall benefit of the team.

Which is to say, I look forward very much to seeing Declan Rice starting up front against Hull tomorrow, and Arteta revealing that his tech-boffins have invented a gizmo which will allow Rice to player 180 minutes in every game. Plus injury time. I kid, obviously, but I suppose we should know by now that regardless of what we think about team selections, use of players, and everything else, this manager will never be even remotely swayed by external noise – and that’s a good thing most of the time!

We will talk a bit more about the Hull game in a quick preview podcast on Patreon a little later on. Because of the book launch, we’ll be recording before the manager meets the press, so bear that in mind.

Hopefully catch lots of you later on at Big Red – and here’s a nice piece on the photos in the book. Just a reminder again that those who have registered to come to the launch, you can purchase the book via the email sent to you (check your junk folders if you don’t see it), so you can simply come and collect on the night. We can also facilitate sales via credit card etc if you don’t want to do that.

If you purchased via the Patreon pre-sale, those books are not for collection tomorrow, and will be shipped to you in due course. There is also some scope to come along on spec on the night, and we should have copies available but obviously priority goes to those who registered. We will then have a final batch of books going on general sale online on Saturday evening after the Hull game. Full details of that to follow here on site and via Arseblog on BlueSky.

#1765. Are you ok, Noni?

Arsenal’s squad construction has given them a lot of depth and diversity in terms of profiles. Timber and White for right-back, Calafiori and Hincapie for left-back. Ezri Konsa has, incredibly, offered both protection and threat to the impregnable Saliba and Gabriel partnership. Bruno and Lewis Skelly, Rice and Zubimendi and Odegaard and Merino for midfield.

Eze and Tzolis for the left-wing. Havertz and Gyokeres for centre-forward. Of course, some of these pairings are more symbiotic than others. Mosquera is probably going to fall behind Konsa as a back up to either one of Saliba or Gabriel. In reality, Zubimendi is only going to play ahead of Rice if Rice is injured or Arsenal have a nice easy game against League Two opposition, for example…

On the face of it, Noni Madueke should really be in that third layer of the squad with Mosquera, Kepa and where Zubimendi probably now resides. The role of back-up to Bukayo Saka ought to have been one with limited opportunity. In a sense, I was always a little surprised that Madueke signed up for it when he came to the club from Chelsea last summer.

I was slightly surprised that Arsenal spent so much money on a player who was always incredibly unlikely to dislodge Saka no matter how much he improved. And how much scope was there going to be for Madueke to get the sort of rhythm and consistency of selection to hone his talents?

Now I strongly suspect that Arsenal would have had anxieties over Saka’s ability to stay fit after tearing his hamstring in December 2024 and missing a few months of football. It was the first significant injury Saka had incurred and after quickly deciding that loanee winger Raheem Sterling was not going to be an adequate replacement, they amended for his absence with a blend of 17-year-old Ethan Nwaneri and surplus left-back Kieran Tierney.

It isn’t difficult to see how Arsenal viewed the right-wing spot as a single point of failure but encouraging Madueke to see it as an attractive position must have challenged even Mikel Arteta’s powers of persuasion. Yet just over a year on from signing for Arsenal, Madueke has a league title winners medal (‘while others are tweeting and posting’) with 25 starts to his name last season, 16 of which were in the Premier League.

In reality, being Bukayo Saka’s third leg has, to this point, proved to be a savvy career move for Madueke because he is getting plenty of time on the pitch in Saka’s increasing absences. This extends to the England National Team too, where Madueke plays the same role. But it was a role that still earned him four starts for his country in a World Cup, including a start in the quarter-final against Norway.

A Premier League title winners medal, a Champions League Final appearance and four World Cup starts was not a bad return for Madueke in terms of playing time. I think we knew when Arsenal bought him that Noni was a talented but phlegmatic player, relentless in taking on his full-back but the quality of his end-product could vary markedly.

In his new signing profile of Madueke on Arseblog, Phil Costa wrote, ‘there’s a feeling that Arsenal lack penetration from their wingers (Bukayo Saka aside); chaos factor, some unpredictability, and Madueke brings this in spades. His first thought when receiving the ball is centred around provoking defenders and driving towards goal, which means you can isolate him without too much focus on the overall setup – you just wind him up and let him go.

‘There are two specific metrics to love when assessing the 23-year-old; per FBRef data, he currently sits in the 95th percentile for progressive carries (6.82 per 90) and the 98th percentile for carries into the box (4.12 per 90). Those are big numbers.’ There was never any doubt about Madueke’s ability to get the ball into threatening areas, the question has always been what he does when he gets there.

Last season, some clips of him harumphing the ball out of the stadium on his right foot went semi-viral. I also think some of his performances were impacted by a lack of balance in the front three. With technicians like Havertz and Odegaard unavailable, he was often playing alongside fellow blunderbusses like Gyokeres and Martinelli.

I admit that my tolerance for inefficiency is high when it comes to attackers. I think attacking is a volume game. The vast majority of attacks come to nothing, the vast majority of shots do not go in or even work a goalkeeper. Individual attacks are the weather but, overall, attacking is the climate. The more you do it and sustain it, the more likely you are to score.

So my ‘we can fix him’ gene for slightly wayward wingers is high. I didn’t even mind Gervinho (a frustrating player, no doubt, but the Bradford miss has become the defining image of his Arsenal career which I don’t believe was fully representative of his performances).

The video of Madueke’s right foot ballooning the ball into the upper tier against Kairat last season has been refined. Both his goals this season have been on his right foot, particularly notably against Nottingham Forest where he cut in on his right and unleashed a low and controlled shot. It might have taken a helpful deflection but that’s because he kept the attempt low.

Last season, his right footed efforts were more in danger of colliding with low flying aircraft on their way into orbit. Noni’s goal against Slavia Praha demonstrated his pace in behind. It was the sort of goal and chance Gabriel Martinelli was hoovering up in Europe last season. European games tend to offer more space in behind and with Martinelli gone, Madueke is one of the few Arsenal attackers explosive enough to exploit it.

Indeed, in my view, he ought to have won Arsenal a match winning penalty in Budapest against Paris Saint Germain in May. There are signs of greater maturity and efficiency in his game. According to WhoScored.com his pass success rate in the Premier League last season was 76.2%. This season so far it is 86.3%.

I think he has learned that he does not have to go for the full-back at 100mph every single time he gets the ball and has varied his game. In the Champions League game against Lille, he sent 15 crosses into the penalty area, having sent six into the area in the game before against Leeds. 15 crosses sounds like a lot but it was very clearly under instruction from Mikel Arteta.

After that Lille game, the manager said of Madueke, ‘I said when you talk about players being ‘clinical’, sometimes that means scoring five in every 100. It’s about generating volume, more actions and getting him into the good positions, because he will decide matches. He had a really big contribution a few days ago, today he had a contribution in the last final pass as well.’

Being omitted from the England squad in September, according to Arteta, provided additional motivation for Noni, ‘After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him.’

He has now been omitted from the England squad again for the November international round. It is a decision I don’t really understand from Thomas Tuchel but I am happy if it continues to provide Madueke with an additional reason to fine tune his game and because it hopefully protects a player who has become very important.

I admit I am not entirely sure how good Madueke is going to be in, say, three years’ time. He is 24 and it’s at that age that attackers typically start to increase their decisive actions. He has Max Dowman in the rearview mirror too. I think Madueke has a really high ceiling and there are small, but encouraging, signs of improvement.

#1764. Denmark vs Norway - prediction, team news, lineups

By Matthew Cooper | 15 Nov 2026 14:52

Denmark will be looking to secure their place in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League when they welcome Norway to Parken Stadium on Tuesday.

The hosts currently sit second in their League A group, just three points above the visitors in third.

Denmark head into Tuesday's match knowing that they will reach the quarter-finals if they can simply avoid defeat.

However, Brian Riemer's side will be looking to pick up another victory, having comprehensively beaten Portugal 4-1 away from home on Saturday.

Rasmus Hojlund bagged a brace for Denmark, while Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg and Joachim Andersen also found the back of the net.

The Danes will be keen to build on that performance, which Riemer described as "perfect", and gain revenge for the 3-2 defeat they suffered to Norway back in September.

It is also worth noting that was their first defeat to Norway since 1998, with Denmark going unbeaten in six games across all competitions before September's loss.

Norway, meanwhile, need to win by a three-goal margin if they are to reach the quarter-finals and they head into the game off the back of a big win over Wales.

Stale Solbakken's side beat Wales 3-1 at home on Saturday, with Antonio Nusa, Andreas Schjelderup and Erling Haaland on target.

It was an important victory for Norway, who were bottom of the group heading into the match after suffering three consecutive Nations League defeats to Portugal, Wales and Portugal again.

Solbakken will be hoping his side can carry the momentum of Saturday's victory into Tuesday's clash with Denmark and they will draw confidence from the fact they beat the Danes back in September.

Hojlund is expected to continue up front for Denmark, having bagged a brace against Portugal, with support out wide from Gustav Isaksen and Andreas Skov Olsen.

Morten Hjulmand and Hojbjerg are likely to continue their partnership in midfield.

Norway could reward Schjelderup with a start after he came off the bench to score against Wales, while Haaland is expected to lead the line once again.

Martin Odegaard was able to start against Wales despite struggling with illness the night before and Norway will be hoping the Arsenal star is back to his best on Tuesday.

Hermansen; Kristensen, Andersen, Nelsson, Maehle; Hojbjerg, Hjulmand; Isaksen, Damsgaard, Skov Olsen; Hojlund

Selvik; Ryerson, Ajer, Heggem, Wolfe; Berg, Berge; Bobb, Odegaard, Nusa; Haaland.

Both sides will be full of confidence after impressive performances at the weekend and we are expecing a tough, hard-fought contest on Tuesday.

#1763. Attacking efficiency key for Hull’s visit

Arsenal are in Premier League action this afternoon, taking on Hull City at home. No doubt there will be some rotation from the midweek Champions League game, with players like Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes, Myles-Lewis-Skelly, Jurrien Timber, Riccardo Calafiori, Christos Tzolis and Kai Havertz all potential inclusions. I suspect Declan Rice will start!

I wrote yesterday about Viktor Gyokeres and whether his good performance in midweek would see him keep his place. On the Swedish international, Mikel Arteta said:

I think everybody was so happy to see, not only the goals but also the performance, how free he looked, how happy he looked, the energy that he could transmit on that football pitch. That’s exactly what we need, that’s what we’re signing, that’s the type of player that can help us to make the difference and he certainly did that during the night.

So let’s see if that means he keeps his place up front. Noni Madueke has had a decent couple of weeks too, with the manager revealing he’d used the elongated Interlull in October to up the ante in terms of his own training:

What he did is he went abroad and he trained. He got somebody to train him and he went into a programme, he wanted to do that. That’s Noni and that’s his mindset – he wants to get better. I love that action that he took because at that moment he wasn’t playing.

With Bukayo Saka injured and Max Dowman suspended until after the Newcastle game, he’s more or less the only option on the right-hand side, so fingers crossed he can continue that form today against a team who are likely to try and make life difficult for us. Players who can beat a man and find some space are really valuable for fixtures like this, and he might prove very important later on.

Hull started the season brightly, but haven’t won since the end of August. All the same, five draws from their last seven games tells you they’re a relatively tough nut to crack, and with a back five they’ll surely have looked at how other teams have come to our place to frustrate us. An early goal is always useful, Ezri Konsa’s quick strike against Everton probably prevented that game from being as much of a slog as it might have been, but we might also need some patience today too.

Some of the difficult games they’ve come through and competed in, they’ve earned the right to be here and been impressive. We’ve been discussing that with the boys on what to expect from them tomorrow and to be clear on what we need to do to beat them.

Arsenal were a bit wasteful in midweek against Slavia Prague, and so making the most of our chances will be important today. Whether it’s Gyokeres or Havertz, and regardless of the construction of the midfield, we need to be more clinical as a team in general, so let’s hope we can produce that today. I take nothing for granted in this league, but hopefully this is one we can just deal with as efficiently as possible before we head into the Interlull.

#1762. Gila discusses his mental health journey, perfectionism and current state: “Changed my perspective”

In the latest episode of AC Milan’s The Chamber series, Mario Gila was the guest and spoke about the positive mental health journey that he’s currently on.

It was last month that Milan unveiled their new series, called The Chamber, which focuses on the mental health of the players at the club. Luka Modric was the first guest, a perfect start in many ways, and the second episode has now been published with Mario Gila as the guest.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The concept, in case you’re not familiar, is that the players are placed in a ‘Chamber’ with no outside noise for a few minutes. Then, they are interviewed by the host Luca Casadei, who focuses on the mental state of the players.

As said, Gila was the guest in the most recent edition and he has a lot to say, having been on a mental health journey in the last few years. Indeed, after hitting ‘rock-bottom’ at Lazio, he found a way through and is now very happy.

How are you feeling right now? [after being in the chamber, editor’s note]

I feel very peaceful, I feel really good here. I think experiences like this are also closely linked to how a person feels and where they are emotionally at that moment. And I think it amplifies everything… a little. I wanted to experience it to the fullest when they told me about it.

I think when there are no outside influences clouding your mind that’s when you connect most with yourself. That’s why I closed my eyes. I wanted to feel as deeply as possible what was inside me and how my mind works in moments like this.”

What did you feel during this experience?

Well, I really enjoyed it because I felt so peaceful. I felt completely at ease, and it was an experience I’ve rarely had before. I’m someone who likes to meditate, to reconnect with myself, and I’m interested in spirituality, it’s something I genuinely enjoy.

“And I felt so much peace, so much peace because with everything so quiet, such complete silence and being in touch with myself, it really is an experience I’m not sure I’ll ever forget. I really liked it.”

Speaking about yourself, are there moments when you’re alone, away from the public eye, away from everyone expecting something of you, when you take some time just for yourself? I’d like to know what you feel, who you are emotionally in those moments.

It doesn’t happen to me often because, whether you like it or not, footballers tend to have very active minds. It’s a profession that takes a huge mental toll.

“But I try, for example, during holidays or whenever we get some time off, to find situations where I feel, well, maybe not exactly like in that chamber, but where I can connect with myself, where I can rediscover that Mario who sometimes gets a little lost because of the job he does.

“And in those moments, well, I feel at peace, I feel that connection with myself, I feel like a person. Because in our profession, whether we like it or not, we lose touch with ourselves a little. And that’s what I’m trying to achieve when I’m alone with myself.”

You told me that because of the job you do, you’re always very focused. I wanted to talk about control because I’ve heard you say you need to have everything under control.

Yes, I think that, given the way I see the profession and the position we footballers are in, I think it may not seem like it, but you have a lot of things to manage. How you behave off the pitch, you’re a footballer 24 hours a day, your diet, physical preparation, training sessions, the physio.

And it’s like… I have to keep everything perfectly under control so that at the weekend or in a midweek match I’m at my best.  So the profession itself pushes you to keep everything under control and if you’re also someone who likes that and believes things should be that way, you take it even further.

“And in those situations, I feel comfortable when everything’s under control.”

Is that just at work, or does it apply everywhere, with your family, your friends, always needing to have everything under control?

I’ve been like that with my family too, with my teammates, with my friends, but I see my personal life differently now. I didn’t before. Because perfection is exhausting.  In the end, so many expectations… Striving for perfection wears you out.

“I think that, to a certain extent, it’s boring. You don’t get to see the real person, their authentic self. So that’s how I’ve been for much of my life. I’m young, but I’ve been like that. Now I’m beginning to understand better that everyone is different, that every moment is different, and to appreciate that more, that authenticity.

Did you used to feel weak when you weren’t in control? Vulnerable?

Now, though, you’ve realised it’s a strength?

“Yes, yes, yes. I understand that people and situations aren’t always as we want or expect them to be. And I think it’s somewhat connected to ego, but now we’re getting into some pretty deep territory. But…I like it! I think so, yes, I used to be like that. I used to be. I’m less like that now, and I appreciate difficult moments more because there’s also a lot of good to be found in those moments.

“I mean, we can’t control everything, we can’t expect everything to be perfect because perfection doesn’t teach you anything. I don’t think there’s anything particularly positive about it.

“In the end, we grow a lot through… or we become stronger during difficult times than during good ones. So I’ve largely let go of that kind of perfectionism. And those incredibly high expectations, I don’t like them anymore.”

But is there a positive side to perfectionism for you? Do you think you became the player you are thanks to your perfectionism?

“Yes. This is a struggle I have with myself, for example. In this profession, I believe that perfectionism and ego are two things that drive us to succeed at work, in our professional lives. Ego drives you to be better than, say, the opponent you’re playing against.

“Perfectionism makes you work harder, train better, take better care of yourself and I think that helps you develop a lot professionally. But there has to be a balance. It can’t all be about perfectionism because it makes you incredibly demanding of yourself and when you go through difficult times, you won’t know how to deal with them.

When you make a mistake, are you very demanding and hard on yourself? I mean, how do you treat yourself when something doesn’t go the way you wanted?

“In the past, for example… I’ve changed a great deal. I went through a really difficult time early in my career here in Italy and hit rock bottom, but with outside help, psychological support, I got through it.

“That’s why I keep saying ‘before’. Back then, I was very hard on myself. I didn’t allow myself to fail. If I did, I was extremely negative towards myself, I couldn’t accept that I might fail or make mistakes.

“Now I handle it much better. Now I feel that making mistakes is part of the job, it’s something that helps you improve, something that helps you grow. So I deal with it much more calmly, I process it much better internally.

“I think you still need to hold yourself to high standards and you also need to know how to find a solution to that mistake, whether in your career or in your personal life, but with much more calm and more kindness towards myself.”

This interview is also meant to share some values with others, right? In those moments, what exactly do you tell yourself to be kinder to yourself?

“Well… What a good question! In moments when I’ve gone through difficult situations, perhaps, after that period I was telling you about, I’m aware that everyone can make mistakes. I know that making mistakes is part of the job and it’s what helps me grow.

“So I changed my perspective. I used to see it very negatively, now I find the positive in the negative. So I understand that if I focus on something positive or look at it from a positive perspective, everything surrounding the mistake changes.

“All that noise stops being noise and turns into a sense of calm. It’s normal to make a mistake and be demanding of yourself, to want to avoid making that mistake again, but it might still happen.

“So at that moment, I believe that being kind to yourself and recognising that it’s something that can happen and that you can use it to improve, is, I think, the way forward to avoid falling into negativity. But instead maintain that positivity and balance that can help you feel at peace, as I was saying in there, like the experience I had in there earlier.”

Regarding that difficult period you went through, which helped you grow and taught you so many things, you mentioned therapy. Could you tell me, not so much what happened, but what your experience with therapy was like? I mean, what did it give you at first?

“I sought help from a psychologist because I was going through a very difficult time and couldn’t find a way to move forward. We’re expected to deal with situations… that I find mentally overwhelming, at just 21 years old, when you have no professional experience, because in the end, everything comes at you so fast.

“So I went to a psychologist, and completely changed my perspective. I mean, I started seeing everything negative that happened to me as a step forward, thinking: this is something that will help you improve, something you needed to go through.

“Everything changed when I changed my perspective. I used to be very hard on myself, very hard, I demanded so much of myself. Now I’m someone who feels much more at ease.

“We can all fail, make mistakes, go through difficult situations, So the way I treat myself, the way I respond to myself, the way I talk to myself, I think it plays a crucial role in maintaining a consistently positive mindset.”

Today, with the maturity and mindset you’ve developed, how do you handle pressure? Those moments when expectations are high, when your heart starts beating faster, how do you deal with those moments?

“It depends. Because speaking for myself, I see pressure as something that helps give me that extra push to… I mean, I’m someone who believes that footballers naturally feel pressure or feel a little nervous before a match, even the day before, depending on the match, some matches are more important than others, but you still feel that pressure.

“I think accepting that pressure is positive because it helps prepare you, but I haven’t had situations where pressure has paralysed me, because I experienced that in the past.

“In the past, I’ve felt that kind of pressure, and pressure that paralyses you is very negative because it’s very different from the pressure you feel when you’re in a good place mentally, which helps you prepare.

“It’s a kind of pressure, the pressure I used to feel, that completely paralyses you, it’s a pressure that makes your heart race, that makes you afraid, so they’re two different kinds of pressure. I’ve experienced both.

“The first is difficult to handle because it’s anxiety, the expectation of performing well, it’s the feeling that so many people are watching you, you have to perform well, you have to play well, and that gets into your head, and I don’t think it’s very positive.

“The other, on the other hand, helps you prepare, you feel a little nervous, you get that slight feeling of getting yourself ready, but if you manage to channel it properly, it becomes something that prepares you, a natural response to having something important to face.”

Listening to you speak and watching you play, I see someone who’s very composed. That confidence you have in yourself, have you always had it? Where does it come from?

“I’m someone who has always given the impression of being very confident. I mean, I’ve always believed I had a lot of confidence in myself, but actually, when things got tough, I didn’t have it because whenever I went through a difficult time, I doubted myself a lot.

“I think you develop that through psychological work, but also by feeling confident in your work. Those things go hand in hand. I mean, it’s not all down to the psychologist and nothing to do with my career.

“No. I mean, everything has gone hand in hand. When I started going through this process, things also started going really well for me in football, which helped along the way. So I’ve managed to develop confidence in both areas, which has made me the person I am today, someone who I believe really does have a lot of confidence in himself, because I genuinely feel it.

“It’s something I’ve worked on a lot, learning to believe in yourself, not because of what other people say or the value others place on you, but because of the value you give yourself. And that’s where I’ve found my stability, my peace and my confidence in that environment.

You’ve played alongside some incredible players. How did you manage… I mean, did you use the comparison with their talent as a way to grow rather than feeling envious, as something positive to help you improve?

“Yes. The thing is, this is very closely connected to confidence. You know? When you believe in yourself and have that confidence, you learn to appreciate what you can learn from others. If you’re perhaps someone who doesn’t have much confidence in yourself, you might feel envious of others.

“And then you fail to recognise the lesson that the other person is teaching you, even when you can learn just by watching them. So I began to understand that when I started reaching a place of emotional wellbeing, where I was more focused on the present.

“Before, because I had less confidence in myself, I compared myself to others more. Maybe I didn’t appreciate what someone else was doing or perhaps I couldn’t fully appreciate what they were trying to teach me.

“Once you manage to build a solid sense of confidence and truly believe in yourself, you see what others can teach you in a positive light. And you see it as an opportunity to grow, you look at it from a different perspective.

“So it’s not just about what people might be teaching you directly. I’ve learned from many players just by watching, just by paying attention. But sometimes I’ve learned from negative things too. I mean, not just from positive things. I understand that learning isn’t just about someone saying: ‘Listen, you need to do this, and I think you should do it this way’.

“No, it’s also about how they behave. For example, right now we have Luka Modric in the team. And I pay a lot of attention to him, to how he behaves, to the humility he shows, to how he handles different situations.

“And that’s something you understand when you’re comfortable with yourself. If you’re not comfortable with yourself, I don’t think you’ll be able to understand that. I mean, you won’t see the other person as a positive example. You’ll see them in a negative light.

And when you’re experiencing a great moment, are you able to recognise it? To feel proud of yourself? To enjoy that moment of happiness? To stop and appreciate it?

“That’s something I struggle with, for example. It’s something I find difficult because I’m aware of it, but I think it’s something that people generally struggle with because we tend to notice the negative things more or give more importance to difficult moments than to the positive ones.

“And I think that’s a mistake everyone makes, I don’t know why. But I’m trying to work on it, I’m aware of it. But I have to tell you that if we were to compare how much I enjoy the good moments with how much I suffer during the bad ones, no.

“I suffer more during the bad moments than I enjoy the good ones. And unfortunately, that’s something I still haven’t learned how to manage or how to truly enjoy those positive moments because we’re also here to enjoy the good moments and to experience them fully. But I find that harder than dealing with a difficult moment.”

I really like how much you’ve grown in terms of maturity, everything you’ve come to understand. So I’d like to ask you one last question to reflect on everything. It’s a simple question: How are you?

Not how you are today, but looking at your life, what kind of chapter are you going through right now? Is Mario happy?

Mario is very happy. I mean, this whole conversation we’ve had has a lot to do with the positive place I’m in right now. If I were going through a difficult time, perhaps there are many things I wouldn’t understand the way I do now.

“But I’m in a really good place right now because I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m somewhere I’m appreciated and loved. I became a father a year ago. I have a wife who loves me very much too.

“It’s as though so many things are coming together, things are going well in my career, things are going well with my family. I have friends who I believe are truly valuable people. I also have a family that means so much to me.

“So it’s like everything is going really well right now. So I feel very balanced, I feel very much at peace. I feel like I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m really appreciated. So right now I’m at a very happy point in my life. Very happy.

“If negative things happen, I have a support system I can rely on. I have that support that helps me feel okay. And I think that’s really important because I believe you’ll always experience difficult moments in life. So there’s no way to completely avoid those difficult moments, you can’t, it’s just not possible.

“And life would lose its meaning. But having that safety net and that support system, I think it also allows you to thrive in every other area of your life. So I’m very happy. Right now I feel incredibly happy, very peaceful, very balanced, very happy with myself too, and I’m genuinely very happy we had this conversation because I’m really interested in all these psychological aspects,” he concluded.

#1761. Arsenal 1-0 Hull: Not efficient, but enough

In yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points. In yesterday’s game against Hull, Arsenal took 21 shots, 10 of which were on target, and scored one goal from that. Efficient?

Despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play. Passes weren’t quite quick enough or accurate enough, but there were moments when we could have found the breakthrough. Gabriel almost got on the end of a Noni Madueke cross which was flicked on towards the back post, Rice had a tame shot from a free kick before a late header which he probably should have done better with.

And then there was Kai Havertz. It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper. I haven’t seen replays but in real time I felt like he should have pulled the trigger – instead he over-complicated it. You have to be prepared to shoot from there, even if it’s on your wrong foot.

Then there was a penalty incident when he complained vociferously, play went on, the ref was then told to go to the screen and we all assumed it would be a penalty. However, the ref said it was a foul but Havertz was offside – and it felt like a massive waste of time. Afterwards, it emerged it should have been a penalty, but apparently the rule is ‘open to interpretation’. So clear as mud then.

In the second half, we seemed to play down our right a lot, with Madueke the outlet most of the time. I thought he did pretty well, much better than Christos Tzolis on the other side, but the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Mikel Merino replaced Rice (who seemed to be on the end of a wild challenge in midfield that the ref just ignored as he tumbled through the air), and Viktor Gyokeres came on for Havertz.

On 71 minutes though, we found the goal. Madueke’s shot was spilled by the keeper, Odegaard was quickest to react to poke the ball home for 1-0. And to be fair, you always felt confident that would be enough. We are the masters of the single goal margin win, and this was another one. Not a day that will live long in the memory or anything, but a 1-0 win that takes us into the Interlull in really good shape, and there’s not much arguing with that.

Or really, much more to say about this game. Mikel Arteta sounded happy enough, saying:

I’m delighted with the win. To go into the international break with a win is one of the best things about being a coach or player, I would say. Regarding the performance, I thought we were the better team, had enough chances to score and make it bigger for ourselves and we weren’t efficient enough to take them.

We then had to rely on generating volume, plenty of persisting until we finally broke them down. Martin then got the goal. Not the most beautiful one, but the most effective one, a simple ‘shoot and then follow the next action’, and that was ultimately enough to win the game.

So Arsenal sit top of the table, with 9 wins from 10 so far this season in the league, and it’s a very impressive run of form. Do I wish we had more attacking potency? Absolutely, and I do worry a bit that it might bite us in the arse somewhere down the line, but for now, we can see that this is a team that just knows how to win, and perhaps that’s the most important thing.

Right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. I have to head back to Dublin today. It was great to see lots of you over the weekend, until next time! And we’ll have an Arsecast Extra for you tomorrow too.

The good news is that Jurgen Klopp seems far from keen to jump onto the transfer bandwagon. This greatly reflects his vision and ability to curb any impulse to seek a ready-made answer in the transfer market.

If you include the loan and youth players, Liverpoolai??i??s squad strength is pretty massive. So there is little sense in buying loads of new players, unless thereai??i??s conclusive evidence that the current crop canai??i??t cut it at the highest level. That being said, itai??i??s not as if the German should never sign a player. In the transfer market, there are 3 types of signings — the doai??i??s, the donai??i??ts, and the ones you sign only if you absolutely have to.

So then, thereai??i??s only two possible types of players Liverpool should be buying in the winter window:

In the summer windows, one can look at options beyond these two. Your scouting team can have a list of targets, clubs are more open to listening to offers, and you have an opportunity to move out some of your own players to make room for signings. You also have a solid pre-season ahead, so that players who might need to be brought up to speed on the teamai??i??s style of play can be worked with before theyai??i??re thrown into the deep end. January simply isnai??i??t the right time for all this.

So what kind of signings should be avoided? Letai??i??s just call them the a Southampton signingsai??i??. Some examples of such players would be the likes of Saido Mane, Marko Arnautovic, and Riyad Mahrez. When youai??i??re forced to play Jose Enrique and Tiago Ilori (who started his first competitive game of the season) as the centre-back pairing, the situation is truly dire. #1759. Strops, scruff, and chaos

I watched Man Utd v Aston Villa last night. When Villa conceded late on to let a two goal lead slip for the second time in the game, Unai Emery threw a strop and went down the tunnel. It’s not the first time he’s eschewed a handshake with the opposition manager, and his post-game interview where he insisted he thought the game was over was very funny because it was such obvious bullshit.

This is someone who has managed over 1000 games in his career. I’m pretty sure he knows when the final whistle blows and when it doesn’t. Can you imagine if Mikel Arteta did that? You wouldn’t be able to move for all the opinion pieces about what a sore loser he is and all the rest. But perhaps Emery gets a pass because he is ‘the best manager in the league’. Anyway, perhaps it provides a stay of execution for Michael Carrick at Man Utd, which can only be a good thing.

Meanwhile, it looks as if Pierre Sage is gonna get fired by Crystal Palace and replaced by Thomas Frank. That seems a sensible appointment to me. Enough time has passed since his spell at Sp*rs for the toxins to wear off, and he’s clearly a good manager. I’ve never been convinced by Sage, I just think he looks too scruffy. As if someone got a 10 year old to draw man and brought it to life.

I quite enjoyed this quote from Mikel Arteta in his post-game press conference after Saturday’s 1-0 win over Hull:

Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game.

I love it as a concept, adding some chaos to our control makes a lot of sense, but it also kinda seems at odds with what the manager asks of his players. Maybe he just means more shots from distance, maybe riskier pass when we’re trying to break the opposition down, or maybe there’s something he’s got cooking for over the Interlull and when we return we see something we never expected. He did kick the shit out of a dugout chair on Saturday, that’s a new enough development to be fair.

I wonder was he referring to the Kai Havertz chance in the first half, when he could have shot on his right foot but tried to cut back/lay it off. If you shoot, maybe you don’t score but as we saw with the winning goal from Martin Odegaard, it might end up in the path of another Arsenal player who can finish it off. Perhaps too there’s a bit of a through line between being more chaotic and what Noni Madueke is doing at the moment. He can be a bit scattergun, but as Nick Wright points out on Sky Sports, his numbers are improving. I don’t think Arteta will ever embrace full chaos, all the time, but if he can add a little more to the mix, it could certainly help.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. A bit shorter than normal, I know. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around lunchtime. Until then, have a good one.

#1758. Liverpool vs Arsenal Preview: Team News, Tactics, Lineups and Prediction

Home » Home 2 » Liverpool vs Arsenal Preview: Team News, Tactics, Lineups and Prediction

Table-toppers Arsenal travel to Anfield tonight with their first Premier League trophy since the ‘invincibles’ season of 2004 in sight. The Gunners top the table and with stuttering performances from Manchester City and a Leicester City whose fairytale run seems at an end, and are in pole position to finish the current campaign as champions.

While Jurgen Klopp’s men are still finding their way inconsistently since his appointment, Arsenal are in top form with five victories out of their last six matches. In comparison, Liverpool have been as easy to predict as a magic 8 ball, with impressive wins over Leicester City and Manchester City, but accompanied with horrific losses against Watford and West Ham. With fourth place still within grasp and with an impressive record against the table topping teams this season, Liverpool would look to give their long suffering fans some cheer with which to greet this New Year.

The Reds desperately need a victory to steady the ship as their erratic and wayward form sees them enter 2016 still outside the top 4 and distant from any title challenge.

With a host of injuries to his main XI, Jurgen Klopp could be forgiven for dipping into the transfer market so early. The Reds have captured QPR right-back Steven Caulker along with Marko Grujic in the January transfer window.

With Grujic returning to his former club Red Star Belgrade on loan, Steven Caulker is likely to be given a run out as a substitute with the current spate of Liverpool injuries.

Ings, Sturridge, Lovren, Coutinho, Origi and Flanagan are amongst the Liverpool afflicted and will take no part in the match ahead. With Lovren out, Kolo Toure and Mamadou Sakho look likely to be Klopp’s first choice central defending partnership.

Alberto Moreno and Nathaniel Clyne should start as full-backs for the Liverpool side and will be crucial in any attempt to penetrate the Gunner’s defences. Emre Can and Lucas should marshal the midfield, while James Milner, Firmino and Adam Lallana look to give Petr Cech some concerns about his goal. Leading the line should be Christian Benteke, who’s lack of form doesn’t threaten this match as manager Klopp has few options in his position.

Probable Starting XI (4-5-1): Mignolet; Clyne, Sakho, Toure, Moreno; Lucas, Can, Firmino, Lallana, Milner, Benteke.

Arsenal must show that they have the one quality required of all champions : Consistency. The task is hereby straightforward for Wenger’s men. Win, keep winning, regardless of your manner and the title is yours.

With half the season concluded, Arsene Wenger must be wishing that he received a Christmas gift from the Arsenal medical team. Injuries have decimated his midfield with Wilshire, Cazorla, Rosiscky, Coquelin and Sanchez out of the game.

There is some good news with Mesul Ozil having managed to partake in some leisure instead of participating in the FA cup victory over Sunderland. Keeping the nimble playmaker fit would be key to Arsenal aspirations, both in this match and for the remainder of the season.

With both Petr Mertersacker and Gabriel available, it would be interesting to see whom Arsene Wenger picks out for his starting XI. Koscielny, Bellerin and Monreal have nailed down their place in the defence and the inclusion of the slower Mertersacker or the inconsistent Gabriel may have a defining moment in the game.

With Arsenal’s midfield woes, it should fall to Flamini to screen the defence with Ramsey alongside him. Walcott, Ozil and Joel Campbell should be the main thrusts of Arsenal’s attacking play with Giroud as the elegant, decisive focus.

Probable Starting XI (4-5-1): Cech; Bellerin, Gabriel, Koscielny, Monreal; Flamini, Ramsey, Ozil, Walcott, Campbell; Girourd.

With previous encounters between these teams resulting in high scoring draws, we favour a repeat of last year’s epic 2-2 result for the same fixture. Martin Skrtel’s 97th minute header in front of the Kop capped a memorable game which also had Fabio Borini sent off and we expect similar fireworks at Anfield tomorrow.

#1755. Interlull musings and shiny distractions

We’re two days into the final Interlull of the year and, as you might expect, there’s not a huge amount going on. The senior fixtures don’t start until Thursday, so we haven’t even got a fresh batch of international press conference quotes to sink our teeth into. Slim pickings.

This time around, 20 of our 25 first-team players have been selected, which is a pretty remarkable tally. All the more so when you consider Noni Madueke can count himself unlucky to have missed out for England, while Bukayo Saka and William Saliba would ordinarily be shoo-ins.

Any concerns about the Frenchman’s absence against Hull, having travelled to Prague in midweek, were eased the following morning when he lined up for the under-21s against Aston Villa in Premier League 2. More minutes in his legs, rather than another injury to worry about.

Bolstered by Saliba and Max Dowman, whose domestic suspension kept him out of Saturday’s game, the youngsters ran out 5-2 winners. Given they’re currently 21st out of 31 teams in their Swiss-style league table, perhaps this is the way forward. Send the big guns down a level and start battering our way towards more club silverware. Relentless madman Arteta, finding new frontiers for his evil genius. He doesn’t just leave his technical area. He thinks outside it.

If you missed it, Max has been promoted to England’s under-21s for this window. He’ll join Arsenal loanees Tommy Setford and Ethan Nwaneri, as well as former Hale Enders Brooke Norton-Cuffy, who came off the bench for Hull on Saturday, and Amario Cozier-Duberry, who seems to be doing well at Middlesbrough on loan from Brighton.

Given Max has been in and around Mikel Arteta’s first team for a couple of seasons now, it’s easy to take milestones like this for granted. But playing under-21 international football at 16 is another significant step, even for someone whose talent has made rapid progress seem almost routine.

Back in September, Lee Carsley described his eventual promotion as inevitable, while stressing that the timing had to be right. The point was to bring him into a squad where he could play and compete, rather than move him up simply because everyone expected it.

Carsley referenced Nwaneri when discussing the temptation to push exceptional youngsters through the age groups. His point was that the aim is a long senior career, not winning a race to the first cap. That seems sensible enough. Max doesn’t need every appearance to become an audition for the next level.

A couple of games against Portugal and France should be a useful challenge in their own right. Carsley and Arteta also know each other from their Everton days, which ought to help when discussing what he needs.

With England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland hosting Euro 2028, you can imagine that tournament already features somewhere in Max’s ambitions. There’s plenty of football between now and then, though. For the moment, let’s see how he gets on with this next step.

Elsewhere, most of our European internationals will be occupied with the Nations League, while the South American trio rack up the air miles again. Piero Hincapie heads home to Ecuador for friendlies against Costa Rica and Bolivia, while Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes face Japan and Singapore, both in Singapore.

I appreciate Brazil’s options are more limited when European teams are tied up with UEFA fixtures, but their friendly schedule does sometimes feel like somebody has thrown a dart at a map. No doubt the commercial logic is compelling, but that doesn’t make you any less worried about tired hamstrings.

Anyway, fingers crossed they all come back with their limbs intact.

In other news, Italian publication Tuttosport has named Andrea Berta the winner of its Best Executive Award at this year’s Golden Boy Awards. The Arsenal sporting director collects the gong three transfer windows into his tenure, the latest of which ended with some fans calling for his head after the failed pursuits of Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez.

Either the bar is pretty low, he’s basking in the reflected glory of the team’s success, or it’s one of those shindigs where buying an inordinately expensive table guarantees you something shiny to take home. The cynic in me wasn’t exactly silenced by the news that Joan Laporta won Best President and Jorge Mendes Best Agent. In fact, I snorted when I read that. And lest we forget, Edu picked up a similar award from the same organisers in 2023…

Myles Lewis-Skelly was in contention for the actual Golden Boy award, which went to Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsi. Hard to argue too much with that, given the 19-year-old was at the heart of Spain’s World Cup win.

Cubarsi also made the FIFPRO World 11. More pertinently for us, so did David Raya. Having finished second to compatriot Unai Simon in the Ballon d’Or’s Best Goalkeeper category, I imagine there’s some satisfaction in getting the nod from the people who actually play the game. More than 26,000 professionals from 75 countries cast their votes, which is a fairly substantial dressing room to win over.

Alessia Russo, who is in fine form even if Arsenal Women are not, also earned her third selection for the Women’s World 11.

As you’ll have gathered from the snippiness above, I find it easy to be cynical about these things. There are so many awards now that you half expect to get one for finding your seat at the ceremony. Still, sometimes it’s nice to give people a pat on the back and recognise a job well done.

On an entirely unrelated note, have you voted for us to win Best Fan Media at the upcoming FSA Awards? You’ve only got a week left. A prestigious honour, that one. 😉

Right, I think that’s as much toothpaste as I can squeeze out of a slow news day. If anything else happens, we’ll have it covered on Arseblog News. Catch you next time.

#1754. FIFA Slaps Real Madrid, Atletico Madrid With 1-Year Transfer Bans

Home » Home 2 » FIFA Slaps Real Madrid, Atletico Madrid With 1-Year Transfer Bans

The ban will start from the July transfer window this year and finish with the January transfer market in 2017.

Atletico were also fined 900,000 Swiss francs (820,000 euros) and Real 360,000 (330,000 euros).

“The two clubs were found to have violated several provisions concerning the international transfer and first registration of minor players as well as other relevant provisions with regard to the registration and participation of certain players in competitions,” said a FIFA statement.

Barcelona has just ended a one year ban for similar reasons.

Real and Atletico were “issued with a reprimand and given 90 days in which to regularise the situation of all minor players concerned,” FIFA said. They can still sell players during the transfer ban.

FIFA said the alarm was raised over the two clubs by FIFA’s Transfer Matching System and its disciplinary committee completed the inquiry.

Under international football rules, players under 18 cannot be transferred to another country, except in limited circumstances. All transfers need the approval of a special FIFA committee.

“The investigations concerned minor players who were involved and participated in competitions with the clubs over various periods between 2007 and 2014 (Atletico Madrid) and between 2005 and 2014 (Real Madrid),” FIFA said.

The ban follows a similar sanction handed to European champions Barcelona, who were unable to register new players during 2015.

Barca were initially banned in April 2014, but managed to delay the sanction taking affect until the transfer windows in January and the summer 2015 by launching an ultimately unsuccessful appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

By delaying the ban, Barca managed to sign the likes of Luis Suarez and Ivan Rakitic in the summer of 2014 to propel them to a treble of La Liga, Champions League and Copa del Rey.

The news is just the latest institutional embarassment for Real Madrid just over a week after they appointed French legend Zinedine Zidane.

Madrid have sacked two Champions League winning coaches in Carlo Ancelotti and Rafael Benitez in the past seven months, as well as being thrown out of the Copa del Rey for fielding an ineligible player.

The sanction could also be bad news for the likes of Paris Saint-Germain and Manchester United, who had targeted Madrid stars Cristiano Ronaldo and Gareth Bale with Real highly unlikely to dispose of their best players without the chance to sign suitable replacements.

La Liga leaders Atletico Madrid’s usually hectic transfer policy will also be put on hold. However, Diego Simeone’s men look better placed to cope with the ban having invested heavily in young talent over the past year.

Neither Real no Atletico made an immediate comment on whether they would appeal.

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 15 Nov 2026 15:11

Gambia will be looking to keep their hopes of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations alive when they welcome Group C leaders Ivory Coast to the Independence Stadium in Bakau for the second leg of their double-header on Tuesday, five days after losing the opening encounter.

The Scorpions suffered their first defeat of the campaign in Thursday's meeting in Bouake, going down 2-1 to the Elephants, and now face another stern test against the three-time African champions.

Ivory Coast have made an impressive start to their qualifying campaign, winning all three matches to collect nine points and move three clear of second-placed Gambia.

Herve Renard's side opened their campaign with a 2-0 victory over Ghana before recording another 2-0 success against Somalia, and a fast start in Bouake on Thursday allowed them to maintain their perfect record.

The Elephants moved two goals ahead inside the opening 24 minutes through Malick Yalcouye's opener and Elye Wahi's strike before Musa Barrow reduced the deficit with a long-range effort in the 38th minute.

Renard has now guided his side to three wins from four outings since returning to the Ivory Coast dugout for a second spell in August following the Elephants' round-of-32 exit at the World Cup, with their only setback during that period a 1-0 friendly defeat to Cameroon in October.

One win away from securing qualification for the continental finals, the Frenchman, who led the Ivorians to AFCON glory in 2015, will be eager to complete the job on Tuesday and guide his team to a 27th appearance at the tournament.

Gambia, meanwhile, are bidding to reach the AFCON finals for only the third time, having previously featured in the 2021 and 2023 editions, and they did make an encouraging start to their qualifying campaign.

Johnny McKinstry's team have been prolific in the final third, scoring seven times across their three qualifying matches, more than any other side in Group C, although their defensive record has been less convincing, with five goals conceded.

Indeed, the Scorpions have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their last six outings across all competitions, shipping two or more goals in five of those games and conceding 13 in total, a record that offers little encouragement against visitors who have scored twice in every qualifying fixture.
